Sailing Africa’s Skeleton Coast with Brand g, and why LGBTQ+ travelers keep coming back

David Hudson November 18, 2026, 1:00 pm PST· Updated on November 19, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
0:00 / 0:00 Instaread
Sponsored by

There’s a stereotypical view that gay cruises are party boats full of thousands of buzzed fun seekers, cabin-hopping their way around the Caribbean or Mediterranean.

As fun as that may sound, it’s only part of the story. Brand g, which launched in 2011, is a luxury LGBTQ+ cruise line that has a loyal following for its more far-flung expeditions and guided tours.

Its sailings carry 40 to 200 guests, and besides the Amazon and Danube it keeps trialing new routes for repeat travelers.

The author joined one such voyage along Southwest Africa’s Skeleton Coast. Excluding flights, all-inclusive land tours start near $5k per person; this cruise began at roughly $7k-8k per person sharing.

For a first-time cruiser, it promised a quieter side of LGBTQ+ travel built around small groups and remote ports.

Swan Hellenic and the Skeleton Coast

The coast is named for old shipwrecks and the whale and seal bones once preserved on its dry shores. Swan Hellenic recently added the route, and this was Brand g’s first charter of the SH Diana for it.

Stops in Angola, Namibia and South Africa, all of which have decriminalized gay sex, made up the itinerary, and the author set off curious but uneasy as a solo traveler.

Other passengers

The trip opened with a night at the five-star EPIC Sana Hotel in Luanda, with airport transfers from Dr. António Agostinho Neto International Airport and a welcome drinks reception.

Many guests knew each other from earlier trips. About 120 were aboard, mostly gay men, many retired from law, IT and finance, aged over 50 into their 80s.

Solo travelers

Not everyone was coupled up: 24 people came to a solo travelers’ dinner, and a few queer women and straight allies were aboard, including one woman traveling with her ex-husband and his new wife.

Some won their places at charity auctions; Brand g has donated more than $1.3 million to such causes over 15 years.

“Not cliquey”

Asked why he keeps coming back, Steve, a British-born US resident met in the laundromat, said the crowd felt friendlier and “not cliquey.” The introverted author agreed, finding he could join any table at mealtimes.

The ship

Small by cruise standards, the SH Diana is the newest and a luxurious member of the Swan Hellenic fleet. Its observation lounge hosted cabaret from Sutton Lee Seymour and Meghan Murphy.

There is a spa and sauna, and the author’s stateroom had a balcony, a video fireplace and an always-full jar of M&Ms.

Food

Food was abundant and excellent, from buffets to à la carte dinners with a standout shrimp risotto. In the small gym, the author ran to Toto’s “Africa” while watching for seals and dolphins.

About six guides lead excursions and give onboard talks that proved surprisingly memorable.

Desert hikes and ghost towns

Highlights included the Namib, thought to be the world’s oldest desert and home to the Welwitschia mirabilis, a Moçâmedes fort tied to the slave trade, and Ilha Baia dos Tigres, abandoned after a 1962 storm cut its water supply and now a ghost town in the dunes.

Namibia and South Africa

In Namibia, the author jogged around Walvis Bay’s wildlife-rich lagoon and watched a fiery sunset melt into the desert haze.

Lüderitz carries a history of diamonds and of atrocities against the Herero and Nama peoples. In Cape Town, the group saw Kirstenbosch Gardens and a cloud-covered Table Mountain, all too briefly.

Sea days

Three sea days brought boot camps, quizzes, talent shows and pool time, and a yellow-billed albatross trailing the ship left the author feeling truly present. Themed parties were entirely optional.

Most ports had free excursions, and many guests paid extra for balloon flights, dune jeep rides or Cape Town wine tours.

Chosen family

Over 12 days, the passengers felt like an open-minded, if privileged, family. Robert Cohen, a retired New York IT professional, recalled a Brand g representative holding his hand as he was stitched without anesthesia after a fall on a Ganges cruise.

“You don’t have to explain anything to anybody”

Mo Bidair, a 64-year-old San Diego surgeon with 26 Brand g trips behind him, praised its personal service, from airport pickups and included tips to staff who fix problems quickly.

He also values the unusual destinations and judgment-free company. For the long-single author, meeting decades-long couples was bittersweet.

This style of cruise is not for everyone, and Atlantis fans may find it quiet, but the author found its calm, and the new friends, increasingly appealing.

David Hudson is a London-based contributing editor to GayCities.
